title: The Golden Age of Childhood Vaccines
summary: After polio, scientists raced to protect children from measles, mumps, rubella, chickenpox and more. One scientist even made a vaccine from germs he swabbed from his own daughter's throat! Then new programmes worked to bring these vaccines to babies in every country in the world.

sections.heading: A Boston School and a Boy Named David
paragraphs: Ask your grandparents about measles, and some of them may remember it well. Before the 1960s, almost every child caught it. Measles is caused by a virus that spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes, and it is one of the most contagious diseases known. The virus can stay floating in a room for up to two hours after the sick person has left. One person with measles can pass it on to as many as 18 others who are not immune.

For most children, measles meant a high fever, a cough, red eyes and a blotchy red rash that spread from the face down the body, followed by a week or so in bed. But measles could also cause pneumonia, a serious lung infection, and in about one in a thousand cases, swelling of the brain called encephalitis. In the United States alone, before the vaccine, about 3 to 4 million people caught measles each year, about 48,000 needed hospital care, and an estimated 400 to 500 died. Worldwide, before a vaccine was available, measles is estimated to have caused about 2.6 million deaths every year, most of them young children.

The road to a measles vaccine began in early 1954, during a measles outbreak at a boarding school near Boston, Massachusetts. A young doctor named Thomas Peebles, working in the laboratory of John Enders, went to the school with a simple plan. He asked sick students for blood samples and throat swabs, hoping to catch the virus and grow it in the lab. Enders had just helped solve the problem of growing poliovirus in tissue cultures, the work that would win him a share of the 1954 Nobel Prize, so his laboratory was one of the best places in the world to try.

Peebles succeeded with a sample from a 13-year-old boy named David Edmonston. The virus from David's blood grew in cultures of human and monkey kidney cells, which had never been done reliably with measles before. To this day, the measles virus used in many vaccines is called the 'Edmonston' strain, after him.

Then came the slow part: weakening the virus. Enders and his colleagues grew it again and again in different kinds of cells, including cells from chicken embryos. Each time the virus copied itself in these unfamiliar cells, it changed slightly and became less able to cause illness in humans, while still looking enough like measles to train the immune system. This process is called attenuation, and the weakened virus is called attenuated.

The first measles vaccines were licensed in the United States in 1963. The early version often caused a fever and rash, so it was sometimes given with a small injection of antibodies to soften the reaction. In 1968, Maurice Hilleman and his team at the drug company Merck developed a further weakened, gentler version, which became the standard US measles vaccine. Measles cases in the United States dropped dramatically, and in 2000 measles was declared eliminated there, meaning it no longer spread continuously within the country, although cases can still arrive from abroad.

Other teams around the world made their own weakened measles strains too. In 1960, the British doctor David Morley tested an early live measles vaccine in Nigeria, where measles was a major killer of young children, and a 1962 trial in New York City, run with WHO, compared different versions to find the gentlest one. Today, one dose of measles vaccine is about 93 percent effective at preventing measles and two doses about 97 percent, which is why many countries give two doses. No vaccine is perfect, but that is a very high level of protection. According to WHO, measles vaccination prevented an estimated 59 million deaths around the world between 2000 and 2024.

sections.heading: The Man Who Made Forty Vaccines
paragraphs: If you have had the routine childhood vaccines in many countries, there is a good chance at least one of them traces back to a man most people have never heard of. Maurice Hilleman was born on 30 August 1919 in Miles City, Montana, and grew up on a farm, where he looked after chickens. That turned out to be useful training: much of his later work involved growing viruses in fertilised chicken eggs and chick cells.

Hilleman was known as a tough, hard-working and very direct scientist. In 1957, while working at a US Army research institute, he read reports of a new kind of influenza spreading in Hong Kong. He suspected it could become a worldwide pandemic, and he was right. He obtained samples of the virus and pushed drug companies to start making vaccine immediately. About 40 million doses were prepared in the United States, and his quick action is believed to have saved many lives.

That same year he joined Merck, where he led virus research at its laboratories in West Point, Pennsylvania. Over his career he developed more than 40 vaccines, for animals as well as people. Of the 14 vaccines routinely recommended for American children in the early 2000s, he and his team developed eight, including vaccines for measles, mumps, rubella, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, chickenpox and the bacteria called Hib.

The most famous Hilleman story happened in 1963. His young daughter, Jeryl Lynn, then about five years old, woke up feeling ill with a sore, swollen face. Hilleman recognised the signs of mumps, a virus that makes the salivary glands under the jaw and in front of the ears swell up, giving children a 'hamster-cheek' look. Mumps was usually mild, but it could sometimes cause deafness, meningitis (swelling of the coverings of the brain and spinal cord) and other problems. According to the story Hilleman often told, he gently swabbed the back of her throat, then drove to his laboratory to store the sample before going back home.

He grew the virus from Jeryl Lynn's sample in chicken eggs and then in chick embryo cells, weakening it step by step. In 1967, the vaccine, called Mumpsvax, was licensed in the United States. It had taken about four years, which was a record for speed at the time. The virus strain is called the 'Jeryl Lynn' strain, and it is still used in mumps vaccines today. Few people can say that a vaccine given to hundreds of millions of children is named after them.

Hilleman's next big idea was to combine several vaccines into one injection. In 1971 the MMR vaccine, protecting against measles, mumps and rubella, was licensed in the United States. It was the first approved vaccine to combine several different live weakened viruses. Fewer injections meant fewer visits, fewer tears and more children protected. Hilleman died in 2005 at the age of 85. Some experts have estimated that his vaccines save millions of lives every year.

sections.heading: Rubella: A Mild Illness with a Hidden Danger
paragraphs: Rubella, sometimes called German measles, is usually a mild disease in children: a light rash, a slight fever, swollen glands behind the ears, and that is often it. For a long time doctors did not worry much about it. Then in 1941, an Australian eye doctor named Norman Gregg noticed something alarming. Many babies with cataracts, a clouding of the lens of the eye, had mothers who had caught rubella early in their pregnancy. He realised the virus could cross from a pregnant mother to her unborn baby and harm it as it was forming.

This condition became known as congenital rubella syndrome. 'Congenital' means 'present from birth'. Babies with it could be born deaf or blind, with heart problems or with difficulties in learning and development. Rubella infection early in pregnancy could also cause miscarriage, the loss of the pregnancy.

Between 1962 and 1965, a huge rubella epidemic swept across Europe and then the United States. In the US in 1964 and 1965, an estimated 12.5 million people caught rubella, and about 20,000 babies were born with congenital rubella syndrome. Many families and doctors were heartbroken, and the epidemic made a rubella vaccine an urgent priority.

Several teams went to work. At the US National Institutes of Health, Harry Meyer and Paul Parkman weakened the rubella virus by growing it 77 times in monkey kidney cells, creating a strain called HPV-77. The first rubella vaccine licence was issued in June 1969. At the Wistar Institute in Philadelphia, Stanley Plotkin developed another weakened strain, called RA 27/3, grown in a line of human cells called WI-38. It produced a stronger immune response, was approved in Britain in 1970, and in 1979 became the rubella part of the MMR vaccine in the United States. It is still used today.

Rubella vaccination had an unusual goal. Most vaccines are mainly about protecting the person who receives them. Rubella vaccination is also about protecting babies not yet born, by making sure the virus cannot circulate and reach pregnant women. Thanks to widespread vaccination, rubella no longer spreads continuously in the United States or in many other countries, although it still causes congenital rubella syndrome in parts of the world where vaccination is less common.

sections.heading: A Father in Japan and the Chickenpox Vaccine
paragraphs: Chickenpox is caused by the varicella-zoster virus. It brings a fever and an itchy rash of small blisters that crust over, and for most healthy children it is an uncomfortable week off school. But it can be much more serious for babies, adults, and people whose immune systems are weakened by illness or medical treatment, and it sometimes leads to skin infections, pneumonia or brain swelling. The virus also has a sneaky habit: after the illness is over, it hides quietly in nerve cells, and decades later it can wake up and cause shingles, a painful band of rash.

In the 1960s, a Japanese virus scientist named Michiaki Takahashi from Osaka University was working in the United States when his eldest son, Teruyuki, caught a bad case of chickenpox. Watching his son struggle with a high fever made a deep impression on him, and when he returned to Japan he decided to try to make a chickenpox vaccine.

Takahashi began the work in 1971. He took the virus from a young child with ordinary chickenpox, a strain that became known as the 'Oka' strain, and weakened it by growing it many times at low temperatures in human cells and then in guinea pig cells. Growing a virus at cooler temperatures than the human body favours versions of it that copy well in the cold but poorly at body temperature, which helps weaken it. He completed the vaccine in 1973 and reported his results in 1974.

The vaccine was tested first on children in hospitals who were at high risk of dangerous chickenpox. It proved safe and protective. In 1984 WHO judged the Oka vaccine the most suitable chickenpox vaccine, and widespread vaccination began in Japan in 1986 and in South Korea in 1988. In the United States, Merck licensed a version of Takahashi's Oka vaccine in 1995. It is about 70 to 90 percent effective at preventing chickenpox and more than 95 percent effective at preventing severe disease.

Because it is a live weakened virus, the vaccine virus can also hide in nerve cells, but vaccinated children are much less likely to get shingles later than children who caught wild chickenpox. Most chickenpox vaccines used around the world today come from the Oka strain Takahashi created. He died in 2013, aged 85.

sections.heading: Hepatitis B: A Vaccine Made by Yeast that Prevents Cancer
paragraphs: Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver. Hepatitis B is caused by a virus that spreads through blood and other body fluids, including from a mother to her baby at birth. Some people fight it off, but others, especially babies infected at birth, can carry the virus for the rest of their lives. Over many years, long-lasting infection can scar the liver and lead to liver cancer.

The discovery of the virus came from an unexpected direction. In the early 1960s, an American scientist named Baruch Blumberg was not studying hepatitis at all. He was collecting blood samples from people around the world to study inherited differences between populations. In a blood sample from an Aboriginal Australian man, his team found an unusual protein, which they called the 'Australia antigen'. Blumberg's famous paper describing it was published in 1965.

Later, Blumberg's colleague Alton Sutnick and others noticed that people with the Australia antigen often had liver disease. It turned out to be a protein from the surface of the hepatitis B virus. This discovery led to a blood test that could screen donated blood, making transfusions much safer. Blumberg shared the 1976 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. He later became director of the NASA Astrobiology Institute, studying the possibility of life beyond Earth.

Blumberg and his colleague Irving Millman realised that the surface protein could itself be used as a vaccine, because it would teach the immune system to recognise the virus without causing infection. The first hepatitis B vaccine, made by Merck, was approved in the United States in 1981. But it had a big drawback: the surface protein had to be collected and carefully purified from the blood of people who already carried the virus. Supply was limited and some people worried about using blood products.

The solution came from genetic engineering, a set of methods for moving genes from one living thing into another. Scientists including William Rutter, Pablo Valenzuela and their colleagues at the University of California, San Francisco, and Benjamin Hall's team at the University of Washington, took the gene for the hepatitis B surface protein and put it into ordinary baker's yeast. The yeast cells then followed the new instructions and made the virus surface protein as they grew, without ever making the whole virus. Working with Merck and a company called Chiron, this led to Recombivax HB, approved in the United States on 23 July 1986. It was the first human vaccine made with recombinant DNA technology.

Because hepatitis B can cause liver cancer, this vaccine became the first vaccine that helps prevent a human cancer. Taiwan, where hepatitis B was very common, began vaccinating all newborn babies in 1984, and in the following years, liver cancer in Taiwanese children fell markedly. Today WHO recommends the first dose within 24 hours of birth, and the vaccine protects more than 95 percent of healthy people who complete the series.

sections.heading: Sugar Coats and Protein Handles: Conjugate Vaccines
paragraphs: Haemophilus influenzae type b, or Hib for short, is a bacterium with a confusing name. In the 1890s, scientists wrongly thought it caused influenza, the flu. Influenza is actually caused by a virus, but the name stuck. Hib was dangerous mainly for children under five. In the early 1980s in the United States, it caused an estimated 20,000 serious cases a year, and it was a leading cause of bacterial meningitis in young children, as well as pneumonia and a dangerous swelling in the throat called epiglottitis.

Hib bacteria wear a slippery outer coat made of sugar molecules, called a polysaccharide capsule. This coat helps them hide from the immune system. A vaccine made from the coat alone was licensed in the US in 1985, but there was a frustrating problem: babies and toddlers under about 18 months, the very children most at risk, did not respond well to it. Their young immune systems were not yet good at learning to recognise sugar coats on their own.

Scientists found a clever trick. At the US National Institutes of Health, John Robbins and Rachel Schneerson, building on earlier ideas, chemically attached the sugar coat to a protein, such as a harmless toxoid, the inactivated form of a bacterial toxin. Porter Anderson and David Smith in Boston worked on related vaccines too. This joined-together molecule is called a conjugate, from a Latin word meaning 'joined together'.

Here is why it works. Babies' immune systems respond well to proteins, because helper T cells can recognise pieces of proteins and then help B cells make strong antibodies and long-lasting memory cells. By joining the sugar coat to a protein, the protein acts like a handle that brings in the T cells' help, so the B cells that recognise the sugar get the support they need. The baby's body ends up making antibodies against the Hib sugar coat.

The first conjugate Hib vaccine was licensed in the United States in 1987, and soon afterwards versions were approved for young babies. The results were dramatic. Serious Hib disease in American children fell from about 40 to 100 cases per 100,000 children to fewer than 1 per 100,000. Doctors noticed an extra bonus: vaccinated children carried Hib bacteria in their noses and throats less often, so even unvaccinated babies were protected because the germ spread less. The same conjugate idea was later used to make vaccines against pneumococcal and meningococcal bacteria, which also cause meningitis and pneumonia.

sections.heading: Vaccines for Every Child: EPI and Gavi
paragraphs: By the 1970s, rich countries had a growing list of vaccines, but most children in the world could not get them. In 1974, inspired by the success of the smallpox campaign, the World Health Assembly created the Expanded Programme on Immunization, or EPI. When EPI began, fewer than 5 percent of the world's babies received the basic routine vaccines.

EPI's first goal was to protect children everywhere against six diseases: diphtheria, whooping cough (pertussis), tetanus, polio, measles and tuberculosis, alongside smallpox while it still existed. That meant building systems to train vaccinators, keep records, order supplies and keep vaccines cold all the way from factory to village clinic using refrigerators, cool boxes and ice packs, the 'cold chain' you met earlier in this story. It also meant persuading governments to treat childhood vaccination as a basic health service, just like clean water.

Progress was slow at first, but in the 1980s, with strong support from UNICEF and many governments, a big push called Universal Childhood Immunization raised coverage a great deal. Today the programme is called the Essential Programme on Immunization, and WHO recommends vaccines against many more diseases for all children. Around 84 percent of the world's babies now receive three doses of the diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis vaccine, a common measure of how well routine vaccination is reaching children.

New vaccines such as hepatitis B and Hib were expensive, though, and at first poorer countries could not afford them. In 2000, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, was created to help. Its founding partners included WHO, UNICEF, the World Bank and the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. Gavi pools money from donors and negotiates lower prices by buying vaccines in huge quantities for lower-income countries, which also pay part of the cost themselves. According to Gavi, more than 1.3 billion children have been immunised with its support.

How much difference has all this made? In 2024, a study led by WHO estimated that vaccination programmes had saved at least 154 million lives over the previous 50 years. That works out to about six lives every minute. About 101 million of those lives were babies. Measles vaccine alone accounted for about 94 million lives saved. Measles deaths fell from about 780,000 in the year 2000 to an estimated 95,000 in 2024, though that is still far too many, mostly young children in places where vaccines do not reach everyone.

sections.heading: Victims of Their Own Success
paragraphs: By the end of the twentieth century, an extraordinary thing had happened in many countries. Diseases that every parent once feared had become rare. Doctors trained in the 1990s in places like North America and Western Europe might never see a child with measles, Hib meningitis or diphtheria. Hospital wards once full of children with these diseases were used for other things.

Think about what that means for an ordinary family. In the 1950s, most parents knew a child who had been badly harmed by measles, mumps, polio or whooping cough. A generation or two later, many parents had never seen any of these diseases at all. They had only heard about them, the way you might hear about something from a history book.

This created a strange problem. When a disease is all around you, the benefits of protection feel obvious. When the disease has almost disappeared, people start to notice the vaccine more than the disease it prevents. A sore arm or a feverish night after an injection becomes the most visible thing, and the danger it guards against becomes invisible. Public health experts sometimes say that vaccines can become 'victims of their own success'.

At the same time, scientists kept building better and better systems to watch for any rare problems vaccines might cause, and to check claims carefully. As diseases disappeared, people forgot how frightening they had been, and new worries about vaccines began to grow. How scientists, doctors and families dealt with those worries, real and imagined, is the next part of our story.

deepDive: The vaccines of this era illustrate three different routes to a safe antigen. The first is classic attenuation by serial passage: measles (Edmonston), mumps (Jeryl Lynn), rubella (HPV-77 and RA 27/3) and varicella (Oka) were all weakened by growing them repeatedly in non-human or unusual cell environments, sometimes at reduced temperature, until mutations accumulated that impaired growth in human tissue while preserving the surface antigens. This was largely empirical: researchers selected strains by testing, without knowing exactly which mutations mattered. Modern sequencing has since mapped many of those changes. The second route is the subunit approach of hepatitis B, where a single viral protein suffices. The recombinant version was a landmark because the antigen was produced by yeast that never contained the virus, removing reliance on donor plasma and making large-scale, consistent production possible. The surface protein assembles into virus-like particles about 22 nanometres across, which the immune system finds especially easy to recognise. The third route, conjugation, solved an immunological problem. Pure polysaccharides are T-cell-independent antigens: they can stimulate some mature B cells directly but generate weak responses and little memory in infants under about two years. Linking them to a carrier protein recruits helper T cells, producing class-switched, high-affinity antibodies and immune memory. Conjugate technology later underpinned pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccines. Historians and health economists debate how to measure this era's impact. The 2024 WHO-led estimate of 154 million lives saved since 1974 relies on mathematical models for 14 diseases, combining coverage data with assumptions about what would have happened without vaccination, so the exact figure carries uncertainty, but every major analysis agrees the effect has been very large, with measles accounting for most of it. Another discussion concerns equity: new vaccines such as Hib and hepatitis B often reached low-income countries one or two decades after rich ones, a gap that Gavi was designed to narrow through pooled purchasing and tiered pricing. Ethical questions also arose: some early vaccine trials in this period took place in institutions for disabled children, practices that would not meet today's standards of consent.
funFact: The mumps vaccine strain used around the world today is named the 'Jeryl Lynn' strain after Maurice Hilleman's daughter, whose throat he swabbed when she had mumps in 1963.
